ci.name: CI (continuous integration)
ci.what: A robot (GitHub Actions) that runs a list of checks on every pull request.
ci.why: A check that only runs when someone remembers is a check that never runs. CI makes every gate automatic.
ci.how: The steps live in .github/workflows/ci.yml. A red step blocks the merge button.

lines: - name: Format       run: npm run format:check
fails if any file isn't Prettier-formatted
- name: Typecheck    run: npm run typecheck
- name: Lint         run: npm run lint
ESLint: spacing, size and the other gates

prettier.name: Prettier (code formatter)
prettier.what: A tool that rewrites code into one fixed layout: spaces, line breaks, quotes.
prettier.why: Layout arguments and whitespace noise disappear from every diff, so reviewers see only real changes.
prettier.how: format:check runs in CI and fails on any file Prettier would change. Editors run it on save.

lines: a comma after the last item, so diffs stay one line

lint.name: Oxlint (fast JavaScript linter) + anti-slop rules
lint.what: A linter reads every file and flags risky patterns. Anti-slop is Omer's rule set aimed at the shortcuts AI-written code likes to take.
lint.why: Shortcuts like 'any' switch off TypeScript's checking. The linter refuses them before they merge.
lint.how: Runs in CI. 'no-explicit-any' is an error. In the game every 'any' is replaced with a real type in the same PR, so the count goes to zero.

lines: 'any' fails the build instead of warning
no 'as unknown as T' double casts
tests may not fake whole modules

spacing.name: Spacing rules (ESLint JavaScript linter + @stylistic plugin)
spacing.what: Rules that demand braces on every if, and blank lines around blocks and returns.
spacing.why: Dense code hides its own structure. Braces stop the classic bug where a second line looks inside an if but isn't.
spacing.how: ESLint in the existing CI lint step. Every finding can be fixed automatically, so one run of eslint --fix clears them all in the same PR.

lines: a blank line before every return
a blank line before every function and class

size.name: Size limits (ESLint JavaScript linter)
size.what: Caps: a file 300 lines, a function 40, 3 parameters, 30 members.
size.why: A big function does many things, so nobody can hold it in their head and every change risks the rest.
size.how: ESLint core rules in CI. They can't be fixed automatically: someone has to split the code, and in the game that happens in the same PR.

lines: a function: 40 lines (off in test files)
at most 30 members in a class, interface or object type

magic.name: No magic numbers (ESLint JavaScript linter)
magic.what: Only 0, 1 and −1 may appear bare in code; every other number needs a name. Colours must come from the palette.
magic.why: 86400000 means nothing until you work it out. A name says what it is, and changing it means changing one place.
magic.how: no-magic-numbers in CI, calibrated for layout code, with the colour rule pointed at the app's CSS variables.

lines: only 0, 1, −1 and 2 may appear bare; every other number needs a name
numbers inside objects count too, e.g. timeoutMs: 60000
the name must be a const, so it can't drift
the palette file is the one place colours are defined

casts.name: No type casts (Oxlint fast linter rule)
casts.what: A lint rule that bans 'as' casts: the code has to prove a type, not just claim it.
casts.why: A cast is a promise the compiler can't check. When it's wrong, the app crashes somewhere else, later.
casts.how: oxlint's typescript/consistent-type-assertions with assertionStyle 'never', in CI. Every cast is fixed in the same PR; data from outside is checked with a schema (such as Zod) where it comes in.

config.source: Planned for the game; confirm on its own run. AppyRig used anti-slop/require-safety-comment-for-type-assertion with a marker nobody writes, so no comment can excuse a cast (ratchet).
lines: no 'as T' at all: prove the type instead

complexity.name: Complexity limits (SonarJS code-quality rules)
complexity.what: Three scores per function: cognitive (how hard it is to follow, nesting counts extra), cyclomatic (how many paths through it), expression (how many && / || / ?: in one line).
complexity.why: A function you can't follow is where bugs hide. The score rises with every nested if, loop and early exit, so a pyramid of ifs fails long before it reaches 40 lines.
complexity.how: eslint-plugin-sonarjs in the existing CI lint step: cognitive ≤ 8, cyclomatic ≤ 6, expression ≤ 3. None of it fixes itself: someone has to split the function.

lines: how hard a function is to follow: at most 8
at most 6 paths through a function
turns SonarJS's JSON message into plain text an agent can act on

jscpd.name: jscpd (JavaScript Copy/Paste Detector)
jscpd.what: Five checks that each find copied code in a different way: exact copies; copies with renamed variables; copies with renamed variables and changed values; copies with a similar shape (compared as a syntax tree); and copies that do the same job written differently (found by an AI model).
jscpd.why: A copy is a bug that gets fixed in one place and stays alive in the others. An AI agent copies code readily, so clones multiply faster than anyone notices.
jscpd.how: Check 1, exact: the same run of words, 90 tokens or 9 lines. Check 2, renamed variables: the same code with other names, 130 tokens or 16 lines. Check 3, renamed and changed values: the same code with other names and other literals, 240 tokens. Check 4, similar shape: the code is parsed into a syntax tree (the structure of the code, not its text) and trees that are 85% alike count. Check 5, semantic: an AI embedding model, CodeRankEmbed, turns each function into numbers and finds functions that do the same thing written differently. It runs locally on the M2, with no cloud service. None of it fixes itself: someone has to merge the copies into one.

config.source: AppyRig PR #25 (G08), #26/#29 (semantic on the M2 runner)
lines: exact: a copy of 90 tokens or 9 lines is a clone
semantic: the AI model says 90% the same job
the semantic check runs on the M2, with a cache on disk

folders.name: Folder size limit (custom script lint/folder-limits.mjs)
folders.what: A script that counts the files and subfolders directly inside every folder and fails when a folder holds more than 10 of either.
folders.why: A folder with 60 files can't be read at a glance, and an agent has to open them one by one to find the right one. A small folder is a table of contents.
folders.how: lint/folder-limits.mjs asks git for every tracked file, counts the direct children of each folder under the code roots, and compares with a recorded baseline. A folder only fails if it grows past its recorded count. The fix is to move files into subfolders that match the code they test or use.

lines: at most 10 files directly in a folder
at most 10 subfolders directly in a folder
the code and test roots that are counted
vendored and recorded files are not counted
fails on any folder above its baseline

aliases.name: Root imports (ESLint no-restricted-imports + path aliases)
aliases.what: A ban on '../' imports. Code from another folder is imported by a short project name, such as @client/pages/page-test-kit.js, which says where it lives.
aliases.why: A path like ../../test/fleetFixtures.js breaks whenever a file moves, and one '../' too many quietly imports the wrong file. Agents get these counts wrong all the time.
aliases.how: ESLint's no-restricted-imports bans '../', and a few extra rules cover import(), require and computed paths. Five aliases (@client, @server, @collector, @shared, @root) are defined once in tsconfig paths. A 20-line script rewrote the old imports; after that, the lint rule keeps new ones out. Imports within the same folder stay './'.

lines: the same ban for import(), types and require
the five aliases, one per part of the repo
rewrote 524 imports in 178 files in one pass
message: "Import with a project alias instead of '../'"
the error text names the fix for an agent

knip.name: Knip (dead code finder) + dependency-cruiser no-circular (import cycles)
knip.what: Knip finds code nothing uses: files, exports and packages. dependency-cruiser's no-circular rule finds files that import each other in a loop.
knip.why: Dead code gets read, copied and extended by agents that think it matters. A cycle means two files can't be loaded or tested alone.
knip.how: lint/knip-gate.mjs runs Knip twice (normal and --production) and ratchets the findings per file and type against knip-baseline.json. no-circular runs in dependency-cruiser, and a second config checks folder-level cycles. Both sit on a baseline: only new findings fail, and deleting dead code lowers the baseline.

lines: an export nobody imports counts as dead
what starts the app; anything it can't reach is dead
Knip twice (normal and --production) against a baseline
A imports B imports A is an error
type-only and dynamic imports don't count as a loop
the same rule one level up, for folder cycles

boundaries.name: dependency-cruiser layer rules (reachable)
boundaries.what: Rules about which layers may import which, checked even when the import goes through another file.
boundaries.why: Layers leak a little at a time: UI code reaching into the server, production code pulling in a test helper. Once a layer leans on another, neither can change alone.
boundaries.how: Each rule says 'files here must not reach files there'. With reachable: true the rule follows the whole import chain, so going round a boundary through a helper file doesn't help. Three more rules keep dev-only packages, tests and deprecated Node modules out of production code. Each rule was proved by planting a violation and watching it fail.

lines: client code can't reach the server, even through other files
client/lib imports nothing else from the client
adapters can't import the code that runs them
production code can't import a dev-only package
production code can't import a test or fixture
no deprecated Node modules (an error, not a warning)

archlint.name: archlint (architecture linter): module cohesion
archlint.what: A scanner that groups a file's exports by what they use. A file with five or more exports in more than two unrelated groups is a mixed file.
archlint.why: A file that does five jobs is touched by every change to any of them. Agents add to whichever file is already big, so it only grows.
archlint.how: lint/gates/cohesion.mjs runs archlint on the production code and ratchets a per-file baseline. A new mixed file fails; fixing one lowers the baseline. The LCOM metric is switched off everywhere. shared/ is not scanned: it is the wire contract, and every schema-and-type pair would count as two unrelated groups.

lines: 5 or more exports in more than 2 groups fails
the lack-of-cohesion metric is excluded everywhere
a file of types alone is fine
22 files frozen; it may shrink, never grow

coupling.name: archlint coupling + hub rules
coupling.what: Two rules on the import graph. Coupling counts the files a file touches. A hub is a file that many files import and that imports many, with little logic of its own.
coupling.why: A file connected to everything makes every change risky. Agents wire new code through whichever file already touches the most.
coupling.how: lint/gates/coupling.mjs runs archlint's high_coupling and hub_module rules and ratchets a baseline. The scan works on a throwaway copy where .js is stripped from import paths, because archlint follows './x.js' to x.ts but not to x.tsx. Without that, the React files vanish from the graph.

lines: a file touching more than 20 others fails (Omer uses 30)
imported by 8 or more and importing 8 or more
and with little logic of its own
JS_SPECIFIER → strip '.js' in the scan copy
fixes the .js → .tsx blind spot; source is untouched
4 files frozen; it may shrink, never grow

stability.name: archlint stability (stable code must not import volatile code)
stability.what: A rule on the Stable Dependencies Principle. Instability is imports divided by imports plus importers. A file must not import one that is more unstable.
stability.why: Core code that depends on fast-changing code breaks whenever that code changes. An import that works is enough for an agent to add one.
stability.how: The same archlint run and baseline as coupling, with the sdp_violation rule added. Findings are keyed 'a.ts -> b.ts'. A new rule records its first findings with --adopt=stability, which refuses a section already on main.

lines: only files with at least 2 imports plus importers count (Omer uses 5)
the imported file must be more than 0.1 less stable to fail (Omer uses 0.3)
a baseline section: the file and the less stable file it imports
how a new rule records first findings; refuses an existing section

p1.title: Casts that lie

rows: const rig = payload as Rig;    // "trust me, it's a Rig"
seat.pod.name;  // seats: [] → seat is undefined → crash

annotations.note: Erased when TypeScript compiles. At run time this line is just: const rig = payload.
Same again: no check, no conversion.
Crashes here when the list of seats is empty.

p1.text: A cast ("as Rig") tells TypeScript to stop checking and trust you. It believes you even when you're wrong, and the app crashes at run time instead.
p1.say: Every "as" is a promise the compiler can't check.
presenter: "as Rig" does nothing at run time. TypeScript deletes it when it compiles, so rig is exactly whatever payload was. It never becomes nil: JavaScript has no nil, it has null and undefined, and the cast produces neither.
So yes, it can crash on line 2. The card shows the empty-list case, where it gets one line further.

failureModes.result: rig.seats[0] is undefined, so seat.pod crashes.
rig.seats is undefined, so rig.seats[0] crashes.
rig is null, so rig.seats crashes.

steps.text: The linter now bans 'as' casts. A new one fails the PR.
The fix: check the data once, where it comes in. A schema proves it's a Rig, or says exactly what's wrong.
Every cast in the game goes the same way, in this one PR.

AppyRig went the other way: 204 casts, too many for one PR, so it froze the count and only lets it go down (a ratchet, like Omer's commit e80b884). Worth one line on camera as the big-codebase version of this card.

The name says what it is; the maths shows it.

p2.text: Only 0, 1 and −1 may stand alone. The gate goes into CI and every finding is fixed in the same PR, so the count goes straight to zero.
p2.num: Game: bare numbers → 0 in this PR
p2.say: Now the code tells you what the number means.
presenter: Omer's game used hex colours; AppyRig uses CSS variables and Tailwind, so the colour rule is pointed at those.

p1.title: The if-pyramid

annotations.note: A loop inside an if inside a loop: each level of nesting costs extra.
A chained ternary: expression complexity over 3.
Cognitive complexity 74. The limit is 8.

p1.text: One loop reads every kind of Markdown block. Every new kind adds another branch, and every fix risks the others.
p1.say: If you need a whiteboard to follow a function, it's too complex.
presenter: Real AppyRig code (client/src/lib/markdown.ts, before PR #24). Its cognitive complexity was 74, the worst in the codebase.
The score is SonarJS's cognitive complexity: +1 per if, loop or jump, plus extra for each level of nesting.

p2.title: Tool: complexity limits

rows: function parseBlocks(lines) { /* 170-line loop, one branch per block kind */ }
while (i < lines.length) { const parsed = parseBlockAt(lines, i); blocks.push(parsed.block); i = parsed.next; }

annotations.note: The worst function in AppyRig, fixed in G06's one slice.
Each kind of block gets its own small parser: one job, one name.
The loop now just asks each parser in turn.

p2.text: Three limits go into CI. The fix is real refactoring: the tangled loop becomes one small parser per kind of block, with the same output.
p2.num: Game: every function under the limits in this PR (AppyRig: 493 baselined, slice 493 → 490)
p2.say: Untangle it into small named pieces, and prove the output didn't change.
presenter: Proof the behaviour didn't change: the old and new parsers gave identical output on 201 Markdown files plus 20 edge cases.
Omer's own G06 tightened in steps (15 → 12 → 10 → 8). With a baseline, AppyRig went straight to 8.
SonarJS printed its findings as JSON; a 20-line wrapper turns them into plain text an agent can act on (ladder rule 8).

p1.title: The same handler, twice

rows: if (!parsed.success) { reply({ ok: false, failureMode: 'invalid_snapshot', … }); return; }
if (parsed.data.machineId !== machineId) { reply({ ok: false, failureMode: 'machine_mismatch', … }); return; }
// …the same two checks, the same replies, 30 lines again

annotations.note: The same check and the same reply, written out by hand.
Fix a message here and the other copy keeps the old one.
A copy, and the file already has a helper called guarded that does this.

p1.text: Two handlers do the same checks and send the same replies. Change one and the other quietly drifts.
p1.say: A bug fixed in one copy lives on in the other.
presenter: Real AppyRig code (server/src/hub/collectorIngest.ts, before PR #27). The same block of about 30 lines was there twice, and a helper that did the job already existed in the file.
Exact-copy detection catches this one: more than 90 tokens in a row, identical.

p2.title: Tool: duplicate detection

rows: collectorIngest.ts: the two handlers are one clone · merged in PR #27
socket.on(FLEET_EVENTS.HISTORY, (raw, ack) => { /* parse, check machine, reply: 30 lines */ });
socket.on(FLEET_EVENTS.HANDOFFS, (raw, ack) => { /* the same 30 lines again */ });

annotations.note: Exact copies found. The game counts what is left in this PR.
Same job, written differently: only the AI check sees these.
One shared helper does the checks and the reply.
The second handler reuses it instead of copying it.

p2.text: Five checks go into CI, each on a recorded list of today's clones. The fix merges copies into one helper that both places call.
p2.num: Game: every clone merged in this PR → 0 (AppyRig: 206 clones baselined, slice 206 → 170)
p2.say: Delete the copy, call the original, and prove nothing changed.
presenter: AppyRig's numbers: the PR cut exact 36 → 26, renamed variables 7 → 4, renamed and changed values 5 → 3, similar shape 14 → 10 and semantic 144 → 127. 10 source files, +113 / −421 lines, net −308.
The settings are less sensitive than Omer's, calibrated by reading every pair on a codebase about ten times his; the first calibration found 0 false alarms in the four fast checks.
The semantic check took 42 minutes on a cloud runner. On the M2 with a disk cache it takes about 2 seconds.

p1.title: The crowded folder

annotations.note: The limit is 10 files in a folder.
These belong with the graph page tests. Nothing in the folder says so.

p1.text: A folder of 16 files. Finding the one you want means reading them all, and every new test lands in the pile.
p1.say: If a folder needs a scroll bar, nobody knows what's in it.
presenter: Real AppyRig folder (e2e, before PR #31). The browser tests were all flat: graph, flow and shell tests mixed together.
The bigger folders were worse: client/src/kit held 61 files and collector/src/adapters 43. They didn't fit the one-slice cap, so e2e was the biggest that did.

p2.title: Tool: folder size limit

rows: folders checked: 80 · e2e split in PR #31

annotations.note: The folder this PR fixes: 16 files down to 9.
The graph tests sit in a folder named for the page they test.
Seven files moved; only their import lines changed.

p2.text: A small script counts files and subfolders in every folder. The fix is to move files into subfolders named after what they test.
p2.num: Game: every folder within 10 files and 10 subfolders in this PR → 0 (AppyRig: 13 folders baselined, slice 13 → 12)
p2.say: A folder is a table of contents: keep it short enough to read.
presenter: AppyRig's numbers: baseline 13 → 12 folders; e2e went from 16 files to 9 plus four subfolders (flow 2, graph 2, shell 3, support 2). 8 files changed, +6 / −9, seven pure moves.
The script counts files tracked by git, so a stray .DS_Store or build folder can't change the answer.

p1.title: The ../../ path

rows: // 521 imports like these across the repo

annotations.note: Two levels up, then down. Move this file and the path breaks.
521 static '../' imports in AppyRig, plus 18 harder forms.

p1.text: The path counts folders instead of saying where the code lives. One '../' too many and it quietly imports the wrong file.
p1.say: Agents can't count dots in a path, and neither can tired humans.
presenter: Real AppyRig code (client/src/pages/flow/clean.test.tsx, before PR #32).
The 539 findings: 521 static '../' imports (client 454, server 46, collector 15, scripts 10, test 6, e2e 6) plus 18 import(), require and computed ones.

p2.title: Tool: root imports

rows: Import with a project alias instead of '../': @client/… @server/… @shared/…

annotations.note: What the new rule found in AppyRig.
The error message names the fix, so an agent can act on it.
Says where the file lives. It can move without this line breaking.

p2.text: A lint rule bans '../' in every import form. A script rewrites the old ones, and the error message names the alias to use.
p2.num: Game: every '../' import rewritten in this PR → 0 (AppyRig: 539 → 2, 524 imports in 178 files rewritten by a script)
p2.say: Say where the code lives, not how many folders to climb.
presenter: AppyRig's numbers: 539 → 2 findings; 14 computed imports in env.test.ts were fixed by hand. Imports in the same folder stay './' by ruling.
The rewrite was one deterministic script in its own commit. The judge replayed the script and got the same 178 files, so reviewers can skip that commit.
Five aliases: @client, @server, @collector, @shared, @root, defined once in tsconfig paths.

p1.title: The code nobody uses

rows: server/src/middleware/validate.ts · client/src/config/env.ts: also imported by no file

annotations.note: Exported, never imported. The file is only read by its own test.
Pulls in a package (and so does react-hook-form) that nothing else needs.
Three whole files and five packages in AppyRig.

p1.text: A file and the packages behind it are never used. An agent that reads them will copy them as if they mattered.
p1.say: Dead code isn't harmless: it gets read, trusted and copied.
presenter: Real AppyRig code (client/src/lib/utils.ts, before PR #34). Three unused files: validate.ts, utils.ts and env.ts. Five unused client packages: react-hook-form, @hookform/resolvers, html-to-image, clsx, tailwind-merge.
Knip found 1,192 dead-code findings in total. The cycles were also found: 1 module cycle and 17 folder cycles, baselined to untangle later.

p2.title: Tool: dead code and cycles

annotations.note: Everything Knip says nothing uses.
Deleted with the 26 tests that only tested the dead files.
A package nothing imports, removed from the lockfile too.

p2.text: Knip runs twice, normal and production, and no-circular looks for import loops. The fix deletes what is provably unused.
p2.num: Game: every dead file, package and import loop removed in this PR → 0 (AppyRig: 1,192 baselined, slice 1,192 → 1,003)
p2.say: If nothing uses it, delete it. Git remembers.
presenter: AppyRig's numbers: 763 lines deleted, 73 added; 3 files, 5 packages and 90 dead re-exports gone. Normal run 483 → 391, production run 709 → 612.
Kept on purpose: pino-pretty (a false positive, it's named as a string), dev and test tooling, and mock scaffolding.
The judge searched the whole repo for each removed name before approving.

p1.title: The layer leak

rows: server/src/hub/store.ts · a leak the judge planted
// server code importing client code, and a dev-only package

annotations.note: The server reaches into the client. Neither can change alone.
A test-only package in production code: missing in a production install.

p1.text: One import at a time, layers lean on each other until nothing can change alone.
p1.say: Every shortcut across a boundary is a bill you pay later.
presenter: AppyRig has no such leak today, so this is an example, planted by the judge in PR #35 to prove each rule fires. The point is what the rules catch.
Before PR #35 a config bug excluded every npm package from the check, so a dev-only package rule could never have fired.

evidence.source: Planted by the judge in AppyRig PR #35; AppyRig has 0 real violations

p2.title: Tool: layer rules

rows: each rule proved by a planted example

annotations.note: Zero on all 12 rules, and each was shown to fire.
Follows the whole chain, so going round the wall through a helper fails too.
Production code can't import a dev-only package.

p2.text: Layer rules say which parts may import which. With reachable on, the rule follows the whole chain of imports.
p2.num: Game: every boundary rule passes in this PR → 0 violations (AppyRig: 12 rules, 0 violations)
p2.say: Draw the walls, then let the machine check every door.
presenter: AppyRig's numbers: 12 rules, 0 violations. Six existing layer rules became reachable, three layer rules are new, and three keep dev packages, tests and deprecated Node modules out of production. 2 files, +124 / −8, no baseline.
It also fixed a hidden bug: the old exclude dropped every npm package from the check (380 modules before, 402 after).
Two known leaks, pages to app (1) and server core to hub (2), are left for a later untangle.

p1.title: The file that does five jobs

rows: export function buildRigMap(…)       // the rig map: who talks to whom
export const STAGES: Stage[] = [...]  // the handoff flow
export function consoleLines(…)      // the seat console
export function buildAccounts(…)      // the accounts screen
export interface Endpoint { … }       // plus types and helpers for all of them

annotations.note: Map, flow, console and accounts share one file. A change to any of them opens all of it.
A constant for one screen, sitting next to a builder for another.
Nothing in this function needs the rig map. It lives here because the file was already big.

p1.text: One file holds the code for four screens. Every change touches it, and every agent adds to it because it is already there.
p1.say: A big file is where the next line goes. Make it hard to be a big file.
presenter: Real AppyRig file, the worst one the new check found: client/src/domain/fleet/views.ts, 5 unrelated groups in 1,404 lines. The lines shown are picked from its real export list (buildRigMap, STAGES, consoleLines, buildAccounts and the types around them).
The check counts groups of exports that never use each other. The file was frozen on a baseline in PR #37. It is on the cleanup list after G15, not fixed inside the gate.

evidence.source: AppyRig client/src/domain/fleet/views.ts on main after PR #37 (cohesion baseline: 23 files)

p2.title: Tool: module cohesion

rows: client/src/lib/readings.ts (new): gb, value, with BYTES_PER_GB named

annotations.note: Counted and frozen. A new mixed file fails CI.
Bytes-to-words moved to its own tested home.
Nothing else used it, so it stops being public. Six groups became one.

p2.text: The tool groups a file's exports by what they use. Five or more exports in more than two unrelated groups is a mixed file.
p2.num: Game: every mixed file split in this PR → 0 (AppyRig: 23 baselined, slice 23 → 22)
p2.say: If a file does two jobs, it will soon do five.
presenter: AppyRig's numbers: 23 files baselined, health.ts split in PR #38 (six groups to one), 8 files, +66 / −30. Knip findings 1,003 → 999 on the way, and four lint suppressions gone.
Kept honest: shared/ is not scanned. It is the wire contract, and every schema-and-type pair would count as two unrelated groups. Seven function-carrying files in shared/ are on the cleanup list.
The tool is archlint, run through a wrapper that ratchets a per-file baseline. It only ever shrinks.

p1.title: The door everyone uses

rows: client/src/kit/RigFiles.tsx · one of 23 files importing coreCall.ts
// the verb name and its result type are typed by hand, in every caller

annotations.note: Every page wires straight into the transport file. It is connected to 24 files.
A typo in the verb name still compiles.
The same verb and type, written out again in the next file.

p1.text: One transport file, and every page and widget calls it with the verb's name spelled out. It ends up connected to everything.
p1.say: If everything touches one file, nothing can change it safely.
presenter: Real AppyRig file: client/src/domain/fleet/coreCall.ts, 24 connections (23 importers, 1 import) before PR #40. The lines are from RigFiles.tsx and WaitingOnDavid.tsx as they were before the fix.
The tool also counts hubs (imported by 8 or more and importing 8 or more). AppyRig has none today.

evidence.source: AppyRig client/src/domain/fleet/coreCall.ts before PR #40 (coupling baseline: 5 files)

p2.title: Tool: coupling and hubs

rows: readRigFile, readRigWaiting: verb and type written once

annotations.note: Counted and frozen. A sixth fails CI.
No file is a hub at Omer's limits today.
The caller says what it wants. The verb name lives in one place.

p2.text: Coupling counts the files a file touches. A hub is a file that is imported by many and imports many, with little logic of its own.
p2.num: Game: every over-coupled file fixed in this PR → 0 (AppyRig: 5 baselined, slice 5 → 4)
p2.say: Give callers something better to depend on than the pipe.
presenter: AppyRig's numbers: coreCall.ts 24 → 18 connections, 11 files, +94 / −28, same verb and input on every call. Eight callers moved to three typed read functions.
Moved, not removed: coreCall.ts's connections were all incoming, so nothing could leave it. The judge allowed it because the new layer is counted and is not a barrel.
The limit is 20, not Omer's 30: at 30 only one file shows. The page registry (22) stays on the baseline for the V1/V2 untangle.

p1.title: The page registry

rows: client/src/pages/about/index.tsx · a page importing the file that imports it

annotations.note: A stable page reaches into the one file that changes whenever any page does.
Instability 0.91. It moves with every page.
And the registry imports the page back.

p1.text: The registry knows every page, so it changes whenever a page does. Pages that import it inherit that.
p1.say: Code that rarely changes must not lean on code that always does.
presenter: Real AppyRig file: client/src/app/registry.ts, instability 0.91 (it imports 20 pages and is imported by 2). The two pairs the check finds: pages/about/index.tsx → registry.ts (gap 0.41) and app/usePages.tsx → registry.ts (gap 0.16).
Both findings are one fault seen twice. It is recorded as the first target of the V1/V2 untangle, not fixed inside a gate.

evidence.source: AppyRig client/src/app/registry.ts on main after PR #41 (stability baseline: 2 pairs)

p2.title: Tool: stability

rows: min_fan_total: 5, instability_diff: 0.3   // Omer: finds nothing here

annotations.note: Both are the registry, seen from two files.
The strictest setting whose findings are worth fixing. One step lower only adds noise.

p2.text: Instability is imports divided by imports plus importers. A file must not import one that is more unstable than it is.
p2.num: Game: every stable file that imports a volatile one fixed in this PR → 0 (AppyRig: 2 pairs baselined, none fixed)
p2.say: Depend on things that change less than you do.
presenter: AppyRig's numbers: 2 pairs, both on the page registry. shared/, the server and the collector have none. No part 2: the registry is never fixed inside a gate.
Omer's 5 / 0.3 finds nothing here, because about/index has fewer than five edges. 2 / 0.1 was read off the judge's own sweep: one step lower adds 5 page-to-kit pairs 0.05–0.09 apart, which is noise.
The gate also gained --adopt: the one way a new rule records its first findings in an existing baseline. It refuses a section already on main.

p1.sub: Every change breaks something. Nobody dares touch it.

p2.sub: Every gate in CI. Every new mess is caught at the PR, and every old one is going down.
